what_it_means_heading: What a tripping breaker is really telling you
what_it_means_paragraphs: A circuit breaker's whole job is to cut power when a circuit draws more current than it's rated for — that's it doing its job, protecting your wiring from overheating and starting a fire. So when a breaker trips, the first question isn't "how do I make it stop," it's "why did it trip." Sometimes the breaker itself has worn out and trips on normal load, or won't reset, or won't trip when it should — and then it needs replacing. But just as often the breaker is fine and it's reacting to a real problem downstream: an overloaded circuit, a short, a ground fault, or a loose connection generating heat. Swapping the breaker without finding the cause can hide a genuine hazard.

That's the difference between a breaker swap and breaker service. Replacing a breaker is a fifteen-minute job once you know it's the right fix. The skill — and the safety — is in the diagnosis: testing the circuit, measuring the load, checking for shorts and ground faults, and inspecting the connection at the bus bar. We've replaced plenty of genuinely failed breakers, and we've also found that the "bad breaker" was actually a space heater on an overloaded kitchen circuit, or a loose neutral. We test until we know which one it is before we sell you a part.

problem_cards.title: Breaker keeps tripping
problem_cards.body: A breaker that trips once did its job. One that trips repeatedly is reacting to an overloaded circuit, a short downstream, a ground fault, or a worn breaker no longer holding. We trace the circuit and measure the load to find which — and never just tape it on or tell you to keep resetting it, which defeats the safety device.

problem_cards.title: Breaker won't reset
problem_cards.body: If a breaker won't move back to ON, or snaps right back to tripped, there's either an active fault on the circuit or the breaker has failed internally. We test the circuit first — resetting into a live short is exactly what the breaker is preventing — then replace the breaker only if it's the actual failure.

problem_cards.title: Breaker or panel is hot to the touch
problem_cards.body: A breaker that's warm or hot, or a panel cover that's warm, almost always means a loose connection at the breaker or bus bar — and loose connections in panels are a leading cause of electrical fires. Stop using the circuit and call us; we treat heat at the panel as urgent.

problem_cards.title: Buzzing, crackling, or sparking at the panel
problem_cards.body: A loud buzz, crackle, or visible arcing inside the panel points to a loose breaker connection or a failing bus bar. Don't open the panel yourself. We assess it same-day, because arcing inside a panel is an active fire risk, not a maintenance item.

problem_cards.title: Adding a breaker for a new circuit
problem_cards.body: Adding a dedicated circuit for a new appliance, a garage, a workshop, or an outdoor outlet means adding a breaker — if the panel has a free slot and the capacity. We check both before quoting it, and tell you honestly if the panel's full or maxed out rather than cramming in a tandem breaker that shouldn't be there.

problem_cards.title: AFCI or GFCI breaker installation
problem_cards.body: Code now requires arc-fault (AFCI) protection on many living-area circuits and ground-fault (GFCI) protection in wet areas. Installing the right protective breaker brings the circuit up to code and adds real safety. We install AFCI and GFCI breakers and confirm they hold without nuisance-tripping.

problem_cards.title: Double-tapped or wrong-size breakers
problem_cards.body: Two wires under one breaker, or a breaker rated higher than the wire it protects, are common mistakes that defeat the breaker's protection — a 20-amp breaker on 15-amp wire won't trip before the wire overheats. We find and correct these, which inspectors and home buyers flag for good reason.

faq_items.question: Why does my circuit breaker keep tripping?
faq_items.answer_html: A breaker trips to protect the circuit, so repeated tripping means one of four things: the circuit is overloaded (too many devices drawing more than its rating — common on kitchen and bathroom circuits with heaters and hair dryers), there's a short circuit (a hot wire touching neutral or ground), there's a ground fault, or the breaker itself has worn out and trips on normal load. The fix depends entirely on which one it is — and the only way to know is to test the circuit, measure the load, and check for faults. Resetting it over and over, or taping it on, just defeats the safety device. Call {phone_display} and we'll find the real cause.
faq_items.answer_schema: A breaker trips to protect the circuit, so repeated tripping indicates one of four causes: an overloaded circuit drawing more than its rating, a short circuit, a ground fault, or a worn-out breaker that trips on normal load. The correct fix depends on which cause it is, determined by testing the circuit, measuring the load, and checking for faults. Repeatedly resetting or taping the breaker defeats the safety device.

faq_items.question: Do I need a new breaker, or is it something else?
faq_items.answer_html: Often it's something else — which is exactly why diagnosis matters. A breaker only needs replacing when the breaker itself has failed: it trips on normal load, won't reset, won't hold, or won't trip when it should. But a lot of "bad breaker" calls turn out to be an overloaded circuit, a short or ground fault downstream, or a loose connection at the panel generating heat — and a brand-new breaker won't fix any of those. We test before we recommend a part. Sometimes the answer is a fifteen-dollar breaker; sometimes it's splitting an overloaded circuit; occasionally it's the first sign the panel needs replacing. We tell you which.

Testing before recommending a part determines whether the fix is a breaker, a circuit repair, or a sign the panel needs replacing.

faq_items.question: Is a hot or buzzing breaker dangerous?
faq_items.answer_html: Yes — treat it as urgent. A breaker that's hot to the touch, or a panel cover that's warm, almost always means a loose connection at the breaker or the bus bar, and loose connections in panels are a leading cause of electrical fires. A buzzing, crackling, or visibly arcing breaker means current is jumping a gap it shouldn't — an active fire risk. In either case, stop using the affected circuit, don't open the panel cover yourself, and call us; we treat heat, buzzing, and arcing at the panel as same-day calls, not next-week appointments. If you also smell burning or see smoke, call 911 first.

faq_items.question: What are AFCI and GFCI breakers, and do I need them?
faq_items.answer_html: They're protective breakers that guard against two specific hazards. A GFCI (ground-fault) breaker cuts power instantly if current leaks to ground — the shock-prevention protection required in wet areas like kitchens, bathrooms, garages, and outdoors. An AFCI (arc-fault) breaker detects the dangerous arcing that damaged or loose wiring produces and shuts off before it can start a fire — now required by code on many living-area circuits. Whether you need them depends on the circuit and your local code, and they're often added when you replace a breaker or update a circuit. We install both and make sure they protect the circuit without nuisance-tripping. Call {phone_display} and we'll tell you what your circuits require.
faq_items.answer_schema: GFCI (ground-fault) breakers cut power instantly if current leaks to ground, providing shock protection required in wet areas such as kitchens, bathrooms, garages, and outdoors. AFCI (arc-fault) breakers detect dangerous arcing from damaged or loose wiring and shut off before a fire can start, now required by code on many living-area circuits. The need depends on the circuit and local code, and they are often added during a breaker replacement or circuit update.

faq_items.question: Can you just add a breaker for a new circuit?
faq_items.answer_html: Yes, if the panel has room and capacity — and checking both is the first step. Adding a dedicated circuit (for a new appliance, a garage, a workshop, an outdoor outlet, or an EV charger) means adding a breaker, but only if there's an open slot and the panel can carry the additional load. If the panel is physically full or already near its capacity, cramming in a tandem breaker or overloading the service isn't safe — that's when the honest answer is a panel upgrade or a sub-panel, not just another breaker. We check the slots and run the load calculation before we quote it, so you get the right solution rather than a shortcut that trips later.

The electrician checks the slots and runs a load calculation before quoting.
